doc.title: Terry Clark — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Bubber Miley and the Rex Stewart half-valve question
summary: Terry credits Miley's plunger legacy and denies deriving his half-valve from Rex Stewart.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Growl, plunger and derby: the trumpet mute tradition

blocks.x: Speaking of vocalized devices in the Ellington band, how much of the tradition of Bubber Miley was conveyed to you in that band?

Bubber Miley was one who created the utilization of the plunger, and he kept ideas – ways and means of using the plunger on a spread basis [Terry vocalizes a wa-wa effect] to play melodies and make it sound almost human. So that was one of the things that those of us who were around Ellington for a while, we learned a lot about that too.

Speaking of Rex Stewart, I don’t know whether I would call it a controversy or not, but this is a quote that I got from your responding to someone saying that you got your style from Rex Stewart: “with regard to the so-called half-valve thing, it’s not true that I derive my style from Rex Stewart.”

That’s true. I didn’t. Actually the only time I used the half-valve was when my valves stick or something. I’m too busy trying to make many notes instead of slurring on a note, except that when I did that little funny thing on “What fools you mortals be” on Puck. But I never knew Rex. I never listened to Rex. As a matter of fact, I hadn’t heard too much of the Ellington band before I got – had a chance to be around it, after – of course Rex was gone long since then.
But to achieve those effects, or effects like that, did you use things other than the half-valve?
I never attempted to use the effects that he did.
Even playing [?]’s horn and all, I never did use those type of tunes, where they “brrt brrt brrt.” I never did do a lot of that.
